title: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards
trick: Recompute leaderboard scores from the raw logs beneath them (whether the grader ran, which trace span was summed, who wrote each action, which evaluator build applied) and watch rankings move without rerunning an agent.
framing_stripped: Called 'the infrastructure of agent evaluation [...] is part of the measurement and fails silently' with a proposal of 'cheap checks that expose the instrument'; it is a single-author (Shandong University) re-derivation of two public leaderboards from their released artifacts (HAL's decrypted trace archives on Hugging Face and tau2-bench's repository trajectories), with no agent run and no model call, that finds four bookkeeping bugs: (a) HAL sums token usage over a tracing wrapper span and its child span, which carry the same response, so 70 of 134 logged runs report exactly twice their root-span cost and 46 report it once; (b) tau-bench grades only when an episode formally ends, HAL's Generalist scaffold ends with an unsolicited message that the simulated user does not answer with the stop token, so 51% of its episodes were graded (Tool-Calling: 98%) and the rest were stored as reward zero; (c) tau-bench's grader replays the gold actions through the agent's own environment object, which appends them to the same list HAL stores as the agent's actions, so grader actions sit in 68% of 2,334 airline records; (d) tau2-bench's re-grading command is a new measurement — an announced banking fix reverses 4 of 136 pairwise orderings among 17 submissions, an unflagged airline criteria change flips 77 of 800 simulations, and a solo-mode name check that misreads four telecom files drops their scores by 59 to 82 points with a warning per call and no error. Plus five one-line reporting checks and a disclosure log (HAL confirmed its three within five weeks and added notes; the archives and rows are unchanged).
method_equations: The paper has no equations; the arithmetic below is this card's formalisation of its prose (sec. 3.1, 3.2, 5, Appendix A), not the paper's notation. Graded fraction and published score: for a leaderboard cell of $n$ episodes, let $G \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ be the episodes on which the grader actually ran and $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ the benchmark reward of episode $i$. The stored score is $$\hat a_{\mathrm{pub}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i \in G} r_i = g \cdot \bar r_G,$$ where $g = |G| / n$ is the graded fraction and $\bar r_G$ the pass rate among graded episodes; every ungraded episode enters as $r_i = 0$. The corrected score adds the offline re-grade $\tilde r_i$ (the benchmark's own reward function applied to the agent's recorded actions replayed through the pinned environment, user simulator stubbed) on the ungraded set: $$\hat a_{\mathrm{all}} = \frac{1}{n} \Bigl( \sum_{i \in G} r_i + \sum_{i \notin G} \tilde r_i \Bigr).$$ Observed (sec. 3.2, 41 of 50 airline tasks whose gold touches the database, nine models pooled): Generalist $g = 0.51$, $\hat a_{\mathrm{pub}} = 0.30 \to \hat a_{\mathrm{all}} = 0.43$; Tool-Calling $g = 0.98$, moved by at most 2.5 points; on write-required tasks only, Generalist $0.28 \to 0.33$, with 23 ungraded passing episodes each containing the required write among the agent's own tool calls. Cost multiplier (sec. 3.1, 5, App. A): with $U_{\mathrm{all}}$ the token usage summed over every logged span and $U_{\mathrm{root}}$ the sum over root spans only, HAL's reported usage equals $U_{\mathrm{all}}$ in 133 of 134 runs with logs; the ratio $m = U_{\mathrm{all}} / U_{\mathrm{root}}$ is exactly $2$ in 70 runs and $1$ in 46; over 133 runs the reported cost exceeds root-span cost by 36.5%; the proposed check is to print $m$ per run ('A ratio of exactly two is a bug signature'). Provenance classification (App. A): the agent's own tool calls parsed from logged model outputs are aligned in order against the recorded action list by tool name and arguments; 'Recorded actions with no matching agent call are the grader's'; 'An episode counts as graded when its record holds such an injected copy of the gold actions anywhere, or when its recorded reward is positive.' Validation: re-running the grader at each recorded ending event reproduces the recorded reward for all 1,951 graded records; replaying agent-only actions reproduces it for 97% of Tool-Calling, 97% of Few-Shot and 84% of Generalist graded records, and 'almost every Generalist disagreement is an episode the grader passed that the offline replay fails'. Re-grade fidelity (App. A): the 1.0.1 banking re-grade of claude-opus-4-5 gives 0.2474 against the official 24.74%. Ranking moves: 48 of 351 pairwise run orderings among 27 archived Generalist and Tool-Calling runs reverse when every episode is graded; Generalist trails Tool-Calling for 8 of 9 models as published and 7 of 9 after; tau2 banking re-grade moves gemini-3-flash from ninth to a tie for fifth.
load_bearing_assumption: That the benchmark's reward rule applied offline to an episode the harness never graded is the episode's true score, i.e. that how an episode ends is part of the instrument and not part of the task. The paper asserts it ('On this leaderboard the difference between the two scaffolds was a difference in whether the grader ran'); the benchmark could equally hold that an agent which closes without triggering the protocol's ending has failed the protocol, in which case the Generalist's 0.30 is correct and the 'instrument error' is a scaffold error, and the headline (a 13-point gap that 'closes to a tie') is a redefinition of success. The paper's own text strains the assumption from the other side: most of the pooled gain comes from read-only tasks 'which the benchmark's rule passes whenever the episode leaves the database as it was', so the re-grade pays the Generalist for inaction exactly as the rule already paid graded episodes; only the write-required subset (0.28 to 0.33, 23 episodes with the required write) is evidence of solved tasks recorded as failures. Second assumption: that grader-written actions can be identified by aligning tool name and arguments against the parsed model outputs — the paper's first rule missed 73 episodes whose injected copy sits mid-record and was corrected on 2 November 2026, the day before the arXiv posting (App. A; ref. [8]). Third: that four cases from two leaderboards generalise by mechanism ('The expectation is an argument from mechanism', sec. 4; 'rests on the mechanisms in Section 4 rather than on a survey', sec. 8).
weakest_component: The Generalist headline is a grading-convention dispute dressed as a measurement, and the per-model numbers that carry it rest on one or two runs. (1) Grading convention: whether an unsolicited closing message should trigger grading is the benchmark owner's call, not the auditor's; the paper acknowledges that the scaffolds 'still differ in design, since they run under different step budgets and Tool-Calling places the airline policy in the system prompt while the Generalist must open a file to read it', so the corrected comparison is still between unlike scaffolds, now graded alike. (2) The re-grade is lenient by construction on read-only tasks (an untouched database passes), which is where 'Most of the pooled gain comes from'. (3) Sample: 'A model's cell holds one or two runs of about 41 records each, so the per-model gaps that end within a few points of zero are not resolved by these data, and the claim we rest on them is the direction of the shift' (sec. 3.2); each per-model row 'rests on 40 to 82 Generalist records' (Fig. 1). The paper has no replicate, so it cannot place its instrument terms against the run-to-run noise its own earlier paper measured (2610.04433: a harness swap flips as many tasks as a rerun, 13%). (4) The grader-action classifier is an inference from alignment, already revised once (73 episodes missed by the first rule). (5) The offline re-grades stub the user simulator, 'so they evaluate the database and output criteria only' (sec. 8). (6) Author position: a single author at an institution outside both leaderboard groups, auditing the Princeton HAL group's infrastructure; the confirmations are the HAL maintainers' (reproduced, disclosures dated 5 October 2026), while 'the τ-bench issue and the τ2-bench issue have no maintainer reply' as of 3 November 2026. (7) Generality is asserted from mechanism: 'two leaderboards, read from their public artifacts over a few days'.
regime: Leaderboards: HAL (Holistic Agent Leaderboard, Princeton; 380 encrypted trace archives on Hugging Face, 138 decrypted for TAU-bench Airline, ScienceAgentBench and CORE-Bench Hard, plus SciCode and SWE-bench Verified Mini for the cost analysis) and tau2-bench (Sierra; releases 0.2.0, 1.0.0, pre-1.0.1 commit, 1.0.1 installed side by side; 2.0.0 cited). Benchmarks: TAU-bench Airline (50 tasks; 41 whose gold queries or changes the database; 2,334 public airline records), tau2-bench airline (50 tasks, 14 with changed criteria in 1.0.0; 4 older files, 800 simulations), banking (5 leaderboard files, 17 official submissions), telecom (4 solo files plus one companion). Models in Table 2: claude-3.7-sonnet, claude-opus-4, claude-opus-4.1, deepseek-r1, deepseek-v3, gemini-2.0-flash, gpt-4.1, gpt-5, o3, o4-mini; scaffolds Generalist, Tool-Calling, Few-Shot (withdrawn by HAL for test-set leakage). Horizon: Generalist ungraded episodes end at a median of nine actions, 'far below any step limit'. Pass bands: Generalist published 0.10 to 0.41 per model, all-graded 0.24 to 0.60; Tool-Calling 0.22 to 0.51; telecom re-grade 0.72 to 0.10 (issue title), 0.99 to 0.17 (sec. 6). Cost: 134 HAL runs with logs; 94 leaderboard rows matched to archives, 44 doubled; one row $149.98 vs $74.99 root-span. Compute: zero agent runs, zero model calls; replay through pinned tau-bench commit with the language-model client and user simulator stubbed; 'a few days'. Disclosure timeline: reported 3 September 2026; HAL reply 7 October; disclosures dated 5 October; author correction 2 November; arXiv 3 November 2026. Code: github.com/YangzeLiu/eval-instrument-disclosure. Venue: none stated (12 pages).
information_asymmetry: (1) Score vs log: the leaderboard cell holds a product and reports it as a rate. Under this card's formalisation $\hat a_{\mathrm{pub}} = g \cdot \bar r_G$, the graded fraction $g$ exists in the environment's action list (the grader's injected gold copy is the evidence that grading happened) and in the ending event, and is absent from the cell; the paper recovers $g = 0.51$ vs $0.98$ by alignment after the fact, and the proposed fix is to publish $g$ ('accuracy 0.30, graded 51%'). The same shape holds for cost (the span tree knows root from child; the column knows the sum), provenance (the grader knows it is writing when it calls the step function; the archive stores one list) and version (the evaluator build is known at run time; the row shows a number). In every case the discriminating bit exists one layer below the published number and is discarded on the way up. (2) Instrument bias vs run noise, the gap this paper leaves and the L1 program needs: the paper measures systematic instrument terms (a factor of 2 on some rows, 13 points on a scaffold, 59 to 82 points on a re-grade) with no replicate, and the lane's killed claim CL-W43-14 and its neighbours (2609.33812, 2610.01618, 2602.07150, 2610.04433) measure run-to-run spread with the instrument assumed correct. Nobody has put both on one axis for one leaderboard cell: the error budget of a published agent score as instrument bias plus run variance plus task sampling. The paper itself says its per-model gaps 'are not resolved by these data'. The HAL archives already hold the raw material for the run-noise half (one or two runs per cell, 'about 41 records each'), so a $0 pass could at least bound the comparison. (3) Where the bias hides in a variance decomposition: the cost doubling 'follows the client path a run takes, which depends on the scaffold and on the model's provider', so on HAL's cost axis it is indistinguishable from a scaffold x provider interaction; the lane's $0 cost decomposition under CL-W43-14 (import S6xF1, on a different released table) attributed cost spread to harness, model and run without a span-level check, and this paper says one benchmark's cost axis 'mixes doubled and undoubled rows'. Any variance share computed on a column with uneven aggregation reads the aggregator as an effect. (4) Grader trigger vs user simulator: whether the grader runs depends on the simulated user answering with the stop token, so the user simulator is part of the instrument for the graded fraction, not only for the outcome; this is the lane's 'who moved (agent, simulated user, judge, tool)' question moved one level down, to who decided whether a measurement was taken. (5) Archive vs training data: 'Anyone who counts actions or fine-tunes on these traces is reading partly grader behaviour, and the contamination is strongest exactly where the agent did least' (58 records with no agent tool call display the full gold sequence); trajectory archives are now sold as a research product and the provenance bit that would clean them exists only at grading time. (6) What the method is not: it is an audit of bias, read off public artifacts, with no estimator of its own spread, no survey of how common the four mechanisms are across leaderboards, and no number for how large an instrument term must be before it exceeds the run-noise floor; 'we expect more of them elsewhere' is its only generalisation.
occupies: Four named, maintainer-confirmed instrument errors in two public leaderboards with their measured effects (HAL cost doubled exactly 2x in 70 of 134 logged runs and 44 of 94 matched rows, 36.5% overstatement over 133 runs; HAL Generalist graded 51% vs Tool-Calling 98%, pooled 0.30 to 0.43 and a 13-point gap to a tie, 48 of 351 run orderings reversed, one model's scaffold order flipped; grader actions in 68% of 2,334 airline records, replay agreement 70% to 92% after removal; tau2-bench banking re-grade reversing 4 of 136 orderings and moving one model from ninth to a tie for fifth, airline 1.0.0 flipping 77 of 800 simulations and one model pair, telecom solo-mode check dropping four files 59 to 82 points with no error), the recovery procedure (decrypt HAL archives with the published script, align parsed tool calls against the stored action list by name and arguments, replay through the pinned commit with simulator stubbed), the five reporting checks (graded fraction, root-span cost with the all-to-root multiplier, action provenance tags, pinned evaluator versions with published re-grade diffs, machine-readable errata inside archives) and the sentence that the grading, logging, replay and versioning code 'is part of the measurement and fails silently' in maintained leaderboards. For the lane it settles that HAL's cost column and Generalist rows and the archived airline trajectories cannot be used as published without the corrections it lists, and that a documented evaluator change is 'a ranking event'. It leaves open the size of these instrument terms relative to run-to-run and task-sampling noise (no replicate in the paper), whether an unsolicited closing message should count as an ending (the benchmark owners have not replied), how common the four mechanisms are beyond two leaderboards (asserted from mechanism), and any automated detector that reads the signature of an instrument error from a score column alone.

neighbors.title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research
neighbors.trick: Treat the rollout record, not the reported score, as the unit of reproducibility: audit 50 repositories (none report failed, errored or skipped runs), document 37 cases where a reporting rule changes success, cost or timing on fixed evidence, and ship a publication bundle declaring views, rules and drop manifests; the paper borrows the declared-drops idea for its graded fraction and says 'Their concern is the rule applied to a fixed record. Ours is that the record and the instrument that produced it can themselves be wrong, and that the instrument changes across versions.'

neighbors.title: Log analysis is necessary for credible evaluation of AI agents
neighbors.trick: Argue from a taxonomy of validity threats that agent evaluation must track inputs, execution and outputs rather than pass/fail, showing on tau-Bench Airline that pass^5 was under-elicited by nearly 50%; the paper adds 'a precondition: logs must say who wrote each entry, since a grader that writes into the agent's record turns log analysis into partial analysis of the grader'.

neighbors.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
neighbors.trick: Audit task setup and reward design across agentic benchmarks (TAU-bench counts empty responses as successful; SWE-bench Verified has thin tests) into the Agentic Benchmark Checklist, cutting CVE-Bench's overestimation by 33%; the paper takes 'the rule as given' and examines 'whether the published run-time pipeline applied it, logged it, priced it and stored it correctly after release', noting 'a benchmark can pass the checklist while its leaderboard carries every error in Section 3'.

neighbors.title: UTBoost: Rigorous Evaluation of Coding Agents on SWE-Bench
neighbors.trick: Generate extra unit tests for SWE-bench tasks with an LLM, find 345 patches wrongly labelled as passing and 36 under-tested instances, and show the corrections change 18 and 11 leaderboard rankings on Lite and Verified; cited beside the checklist as the other audit of whether the grading rule is right (paraphrase of sec. 7: 'Both examine whether the benchmark's grading rule is right'), against which this paper's errors are in applying a rule already taken as correct.

neighbors.title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly
neighbors.trick: Run five models through three production coding harnesses on SWE-bench Verified and rerun identical configurations: on a 45-task hard subset a harness swap flips as many tasks as a rerun (13% both), harness cost differs up to 3x and is set by the per-step preamble, and 447 tasks resolve only a 5-point gap; the same authors cite it as a prior 'separation of instrument from model' where 'a single pass rate is the wrong instrument for telling harnesses apart' — it is also the run-noise measurement this paper lacks.

theme_fit.why: benchmark validity, cost accounting and leaderboard churn measured from released artifacts; names the grader, tracer, archiver and evaluator version as parties that move an outcome, directly extending the lane's 'who moved' question and the L1 program's noise-floor claim with a bias term it never had

the cost error is a tracing-span aggregation bug (parent and child span carrying the same usage block), a systems detail with no serving or rollout-engine content; same words ('cost', 'input tokens'), different problem
no training; the only training-side content is a warning that fine-tuning on the archived traces learns grader actions

limitations_as_complaints: I audited two leaderboards and I am asking you to believe the class is everywhere on the strength of the mechanism alone: 'Our evidence comes from two leaderboards and the benchmarks they host, and the expectation that similar errors are common elsewhere rests on the mechanisms in Section 4 rather than on a survey.' (sec. 8); 'The expectation is an argument from mechanism.' (sec. 4). Nobody has counted how many public agent leaderboards gate grading on termination, nest tracing spans, replay gold through the agent's environment or re-grade across evaluator versions.

My offline re-grade of the ungraded half runs with the simulated user removed, so it scores the database and the output rule and nothing a user would have said or asked: 'The HAL re-grades use the τ-bench commit HAL's setup pins with the user simulator stubbed, so they evaluate the database and output criteria only.' (sec. 8). And the benchmark owners have not told me whether an unsolicited closing message is an ending or a failure: 'As of 3 November 2026 the τ-bench issue and the τ2-bench issue have no maintainer reply' (sec. 3.5).

I can give you the direction of the shift and not its size against run noise, because every cell is one or two runs: 'A model's cell holds one or two runs of about 41 records each, so the per-model gaps that end within a few points of zero are not resolved by these data, and the claim we rest on them is the direction of the shift.' (sec. 3.2). My own earlier paper measured a harness swap flipping as many tasks as a rerun (13%, 2610.04433) and this paper never puts the instrument terms it found on that scale.
